name: collapse-recovery
description: Chapter 7: Drive an idle employee's need gauges to collapse via nothing but time passing. Finding #11: the original claim ("verify rest restores them to resume original task") does not hold at this file's own tick budget — a real run confirms collapse is genuine (collapsedCount 0->1, wellBeing craters) but the employee is STILL collapsing at tick 350, not recovered; extending the run to 2350 ticks shows repeated collapse/rest cycles (hunger, fatigue, and breakNeed each collapse and recover on their own, different-length cycles) draining cash via NEED_REST_COSTS on every cycle, ending in bankruptcy + worker_revolt (LEVEL LOSS) rather than a clean recovery. Whether that's an unbalanced interaction (idle need-drain, tickNeedGauges via events.ts, keeps draining at the idle rate even while a rest action is in progress, so a short/weak rest may net-lose ground) or intended difficulty for a company that hires someone and gives them no work is a design question — filed as a follow-up, not decided here. This file now asserts only what a real run verifies: collapse is real, recovery within 350 ticks is not.

steps.description: 'bunkhouse' was never a valid build type (NEED_REST_BUILDING_TYPES maps every need to 'living_quarters' — dedicated canteen/bunkhouse/break_room types don't exist yet); this file already uses the real type. The employee hires far from this build site (spawn (82,34) vs building (5,5) on this seed's dusty_hollow map, real distance ~82 tiles) — real, not a scenario mistake, and part of why the rest cycle below struggles to keep up.

expect.note: baseline before the idle-drain run below — not yet collapsing, fresh hire's needs start full
250 ticks of pure idle need-drain (no drill plan, nothing to do) is enough to collapse a fresh hire — real, verified via a direct engine run, not assumed from the file's own claim
Finding #11: still collapsing at tick 350, not recovered — the original file's claim ("rest restores them") does not hold within this budget; wellBeing keeps cratering rather than climbing back
